opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's both, and the tension between the two framings is actually productive.

Multimodal large models have given robotics something we never had before: a strong prior about the world. When a model has seen billions of images and read a huge amount of text, it already knows what a cup is, that you hold it by the handle, that you shouldn't put a phone in the microwave. Ten years ago, we had to engineer all of that by hand or learn it from scratch with very little data. So building on top of vision-language models has been a big accelerator, and I don't think anyone serious would throw that away.

But I don't think robotics is just "add an action head to a VLM." There are a few things that make it fundamentally different.

The first is the data. Language and vision models learn from the internet, which is enormous and essentially free. There is no internet of robot actions. Every trajectory has to be collected through teleoperation, simulation, or the robot's own experience, and that's expensive and slow. So questions like how to scale data, how to transfer across different robot bodies, and how to use simulation well are core research problems that don't exist in the same form for multimodal models.

The second is the physical world itself. A language model can be wrong and you just regenerate. A robot that's wrong drops the object, breaks something, or hurts someone. You're dealing with contact, friction, dynamics, latency, and closed-loop control at high frequency. Reasoning about "what" to do is something VLMs help with; knowing "how" to do it with your body, in real time, is a different kind of intelligence, closer to motor skill than to knowledge.

The third is embodiment. Different robots have different arms, hands, sensors, and degrees of freedom. A foundation model for robotics has to deal with that diversity in a way a text model never does.

So my view is: the foundation of robotics models will keep borrowing heavily from multimodal models, especially for perception, semantics, and high-level reasoning. But the parts that touch the physical world, action representation, control, data flywheels, safety, sim-to-real, those need their own discipline, their own benchmarks, and their own people who deeply understand physics and hardware. If we treat robotics only as an extension, we'll end up with robots that can describe a task beautifully but still can't do it reliably. And reliability in the real world is the whole game.

r001.rationale: It says VLMs help with deciding what to do, while executing actions with a robot body requires distinct motor skill and control, making clear that current multimodal models do not provide that capability on their own.

r002.rationale: It says robotics has borrowed from and built on multimodal models, but does not state that most current VLA or robot large-model work consists of fine-tuning existing models.

r003.rationale: It argues robotics needs its own discipline, but does not make that independence contingent on existing approaches reaching bottlenecks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's a bit of both, and the framing of "independent versus extension" is probably less useful than asking what actually transfers and what doesn't.

What transfers is enormous. The reason robotics has moved so fast in the last few years is precisely because we stopped treating it as an island. Vision-language models give you semantic understanding of the world essentially for free. You get object recognition, scene understanding, instruction following, some commonsense reasoning. Ten years ago each of those was its own robotics subfield with its own benchmarks. So in that sense, yes, robot foundation models are downstream of the multimodal revolution, and anyone who says otherwise is ignoring where the capability came from.

But I don't think that makes robotics merely an extension, and here's why. Language and vision models learn from data that already exists on the internet. Robotics has to generate its own data, and the process of generating that data is itself the hard research problem. The action space is continuous, it's high-frequency, it's embodiment-specific, and the consequences of a mistake are physical. A language model can hallucinate a sentence and nobody gets hurt. A robot that hallucinates a grasp drops a glass or, worse, hurts a person. That changes what you optimize for. It changes how you think about closed-loop control, about latency, about uncertainty, about safety. Those are not problems you inherit from the multimodal stack. You have to solve them yourself.

So my view is that robotics will end up looking more like a discipline that sits on top of multimodal models but has its own first principles. The analogy I sometimes use is physics and engineering. Engineering uses physics constantly, but nobody would say mechanical engineering is just applied physics. It has its own questions, its own methods, its own notion of what good work looks like.

And practically, I think this matters for how we train people and how we organize research. If you treat robotics as a footnote to LLMs, you end up with people who can fine-tune a VLA but have never thought about contact dynamics or what happens when the policy runs at ten hertz instead of a hundred. If you treat it as fully independent, you reinvent things the language community already solved. The interesting work right now is at the seam, and I'd rather we keep it that way than draw a hard line in either direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes robotics’ distinctive action, control, and safety challenges, but does not clearly say that current multimodal models lack the capability to output robot actions.

r002.rationale: It mentions fine-tuning a VLA as an example, but does not state that most current work on VLA or robot large models consists of fine-tuning existing language or multimodal models.

r003.rationale: It says robotics may develop its own first principles, but does not make that independence conditional on existing approaches reaching bottlenecks.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics deserves its own research agenda, but I wouldn’t draw a hard boundary between it and multimodal models. The important question is what changes when a model has to act in the physical world.

A multimodal model can understand an image or explain how to pick up a cup. A robot has to decide where to move, how much force to apply, and what to do when the cup slips. Its actions change the observations it receives next. That closed loop, together with physical constraints and the consequences of mistakes, introduces problems that understanding images and language alone doesn’t solve.

The data problem is also different. We have a lot of text and video, but video generally doesn’t tell you the exact action, force, or contact conditions that produced an outcome. So learning from robot experience, using simulation, and transferring across different bodies become central questions.

At the same time, multimodal models provide a valuable starting point: semantic knowledge, instruction understanding, and representations that can transfer across tasks. We should build on those capabilities while studying what is missing for reliable action.

So I’d frame robotics foundation models as a distinct research direction with strong connections to multimodal learning. Whether we call it an independent discipline matters less than whether our methods let robots learn broadly and operate reliably in unfamiliar situations.

r001.rationale: It contrasts multimodal models that understand or explain with robots that must choose and execute physical actions, identifying action as a capability that understanding alone does not provide.

r002.rationale: It does not state that most vision-language-action or robot large-model work fine-tunes existing language or multimodal models.

r003.rationale: It calls robotics a distinct research direction, but does not make that independence conditional on existing approaches encountering bottlenecks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an important distinction between saying robotics needs its own research agenda and saying it should be a completely separate discipline. I agree with the first, but I’m less convinced by the second.

A robot doesn’t just interpret information—it takes actions that change the world. Those actions affect what it observes next. So the central problem is a closed loop of perception, action, and feedback, with physical constraints and consequences. A model can describe how to pick up a cup very convincingly and still fail to grasp it. That gap is fundamental.

This means robotics foundation models need capabilities and evaluation methods that go beyond those of multimodal language models. We need to ask whether a robot can complete a task, recover when something goes wrong, and generalize to a different environment or a different body. We also need to address how it learns from interaction, because collecting physical experience is much more expensive than collecting text or images.

But none of that means we should discard the progress in multimodal models. Their representations, semantic knowledge, and ability to interpret instructions can be extremely useful. The question is how to connect those strengths to reliable physical behavior.

So I would give robotics intellectual independence without insisting on isolation. If we treat it merely as another output modality, we underestimate the problem. If we draw a rigid boundary around it, we risk losing useful ideas. The real test is whether our models can act successfully in the world.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes interpreting information from taking physical actions and says multimodal language models can describe an action yet fail to perform it, identifying physical action as a missing capability.

r002.rationale: It does not state that most current vision-language-action or robot large models are fine-tuned from existing language or multimodal models.

r003.rationale: It argues for robotics having intellectual independence, but does not condition greater independence on existing approaches encountering bottlenecks.
